intro:
John writes 3 John around AD 85-95 to his dear friend Gaius—a faithful church member known for his hospitality to traveling missionaries. This personal letter reveals church politics: a domineering leader named Diotrephes refuses to welcome John's representatives, spreads malicious gossip, and even excommunicates those who show hospitality to brothers he disapproves of.

The situation shows early church tension between centralized authority and local autonomy. Diotrephes loves 'to be first' and rejects apostolic authority, while Gaius represents faithful cooperation. John commends Demetrius (likely the letter carrier) as reliable, contrasting with Diotrephes' self-promotion.

This is the most personal New Testament letter—addressing individual conflicts rather than theological issues. John writes as an elder appealing to a loyal friend, promising to confront Diotrephes personally when he visits. The letter demonstrates that early churches faced leadership struggles not unlike modern congregations.
outro:
John ends hoping to see Gaius soon, sending peace greetings, and asking Gaius to greet friends by name. The personal tone shows deep relationships within early Christian networks.

3 John provides rare insight into early church administration and conflict. Its warning against leaders who 'love to be first' remains relevant for churches of all sizes. The commendation of Gaius' hospitality—supporting missionaries 'in a manner worthy of God'—established patterns for missionary support.

This brief letter balances truth and love in church relationships. Written amid personal conflict, it shows apostolic authority exercised through persuasion rather than command, through commendation of the faithful rather than only condemnation of the problematic.
